transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Um… I guess I came in because my communication has been getting a little hard to follow, apparently. I’m an artist, so I know I can be kind of associative, and usually that’s a good thing, but lately my artist statements and client notes—and even when I’m talking in meetings—start jumping around. Like I’ll go from textures to budgets to… meanings I’m seeing in things, and people keep saying they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain.  

I don’t know if that makes sense, or if I’m explaining it right.
Have you been feeling unusually high, energized, or euphoric lately?

Yeah… I mean, not “euphoric” like partying or anything. But I do get these stretches where I feel really lit up, like everything is connecting and every idea I have is kind of… brilliant, or at least it feels that way in the moment.

And I can feel almost unstoppable, which sounds dramatic, sorry. But then if someone makes a small comment—like a collaborator questioning something—I can snap back way harder than I mean to. It feels bigger than the situation, and then I feel embarrassed after. Does that answer it okay?
When you’re in those lit-up, unstoppable stretches, do you need much less sleep than usual?

A little, yeah. I mean, I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, but when I’m in that mode I can work really late, sleep maybe two or three hours, and then wake up feeling… bright, I guess? Like ready to keep going.

It’s not like my normal tired the next day thing, which is probably the part that seems a little unusual. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Have you been hearing voices or seeing things that other people don’t seem to hear or see?

Um… a little, I guess. I don’t want to overstate it, because it’s not all the time.

When I’m alone in my studio, sometimes I’ll hear what sounds like a woman quietly commenting, like from behind the shelves. And I’ll turn to check, and no one’s there. There’s also been a couple times where I smell this really strong hot-metal smell near an unfinished piece, and it feels completely real in the moment… but then I check and there’s no source for it.

I know that probably sounds strange. I’m not trying to be dramatic—I just… that’s what happens sometimes.
Do the voice and hot-metal smell ever happen when you’re not in one of those lit-up, unstoppable periods?

Yeah… I think so. I was hoping it was only during those high-energy stretches, because that would make more sense to me, but there was this quieter month where I was sleeping more normally and I didn’t feel especially unstoppable or anything.

And I still heard the comments sometimes, like from behind the shelves. It wasn’t constant, and I tried not to make a big deal of it. But it went on for a few weeks. I also caught myself reading these… hidden warnings, I guess, into ordinary studio materials. Like things that were probably just normal objects or supplies, but they felt like they were telling me something.

I know that sounds odd. I’m saying it okay?
Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing the voice or noticing those hidden warnings while not feeling unusually energized or 'lit up'?

Yeah… yes, I think that did happen. There was that quieter month I mentioned, where I was sleeping more normally and I wasn’t feeling especially revved up or unstoppable.

But even then, for several weeks, I was still hearing those little comments from behind the shelves sometimes, and I kept… reading these hidden warnings into normal studio materials. I tried to tell myself it was nothing, so I don’t want to make it sound bigger than it was, but it was more than two weeks. Is that the kind of separation you’re asking about?
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I’m… not sure I can say that clearly. I’ve had low stretches, definitely, but whether it was most of the day nearly every day for two full weeks… I don’t want to answer wrong or make it sound more certain than it is.

Can you maybe tell me what you mean by “depressed” in that question? Like, how low does it have to be to count?
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt down or unable to enjoy things most of the day nearly every day?

I’m honestly not sure. I’ve had times where I felt kind of flat or down, and things didn’t feel as easy to enjoy, but I don’t know if it was most of the day nearly every day for two weeks.

I don’t want to overstate it just to give you a neat answer. Maybe… maybe not? I can remember low patches, but I’m not confident they fit exactly what you’re asking.
Compared with before all this started, has your work or day-to-day functioning gotten noticeably worse?

Yeah… I mean, I’d like to say I’ve mostly kept things together, and in some ways I have, but it has gotten worse.

I’ve missed some paid deadlines, which is embarrassing. And in meetings I think I’ve confused collaborators because my notes or explanations weren’t really landing. There was also an exhibition that got postponed because the notes and proposals I turned in just… didn’t make enough sense to use.

I don’t know if that counts as “noticeably worse,” but compared to before, yes, I think it probably is.
Before these experiences began, did you have any seizure, head injury, or other neurological illness?

Not that I know of. I don’t think I’ve ever had seizures or a major head injury or anything neurological like that before this started.

I mean, unless there’s something minor I’m not thinking of, but nothing diagnosed or serious that I’m aware of.
During any low period, did you ever lose interest or pleasure in almost everything you usually enjoy?

I don’t think it was almost everything, no. I mean, there were times things felt kind of muted, like I wasn’t as excited about work or seeing people, but I could still enjoy some things here and there.

So… I don’t want to say yes if that makes it sound more complete than it was. Maybe less interested than usual, but not like pleasure was gone from everything.
From when the voice and those hidden warnings first began, has there ever been a six-month period when those experiences or the related problems with your thinking and communication were going on?

I think… yes. I mean, not constantly every single day, but if you’re asking whether there’s been a stretch that long where the messages in materials and the voice, or sometimes the smells in the studio, were still happening or affecting how I was thinking and explaining things… then yes.

It’s been about eleven months altogether, I think. I’m not sure I’ve been tracking it perfectly, but it’s definitely more than six months.
At any time, have you had two weeks or longer when you felt down most of the day nearly every day?

I’m not totally sure. I’ve had some down stretches, but I don’t know if it was most of the day nearly every day for a full two weeks. I wouldn’t want to exaggerate it.

Maybe there were periods where I felt low or discouraged, but I’m not sure it fits exactly the way you’re asking.
Have you ever had a period of at least one week when you felt unusually energized or unstoppable most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I wouldn’t want to make it sound dramatic, but there have been stretches where I feel really lit up, like I can do anything and every idea I’m having is kind of brilliant.

And it can last… around a week, maybe more. Most of the day, yes. I usually think of it as being productive or inspired, which sounds better, but sometimes it gets intense. Like if a collaborator makes one small comment, I can snap more than makes sense for the situation. Then afterward I feel embarrassed, because I don’t want to be that kind of person.
When the voice or hidden warnings happen, do they ever occur only during those energized, lit-up periods?

No… I don’t think only then.

There was actually a quieter month where I was sleeping more normally and I didn’t feel unstoppable or especially lit up. But I still heard comments like they were coming from behind the shelves, and I was still reading hidden warnings into regular studio materials for several weeks.

I know that probably sounds strange, but… yeah, it wasn’t only during the energized periods.
Over the whole time these symptoms have been going on, have the energized or low mood periods made up most of the illness?

I think… yes, if I’m being honest. I don’t want to overstate it, because it’s not like I’m at the same level all the time.

But looking back over the year, the more energized or irritable, overproductive stretches probably take up more space than the calmer stretches do. It rises and falls, but those periods are there a lot. Does that answer what you mean?

patient.answer:
I think… yes, if I’m being honest. I don’t want to overstate it, because it’s not like I’m at the same level all the time.

But looking back over the year, the more energized or irritable, overproductive stretches probably take up more space than the calmer stretches do. It rises and falls, but those periods are there a lot. Does that answer what you mean?

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms persisted for >2 weeks outside mood episodes, ruling out F31.2; mood episodes (energized/irritable periods) have been present for a substantial portion of the illness, favoring schizoaffective disorder over F20.9.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a manic syndrome with elevated/expansive energy, decreased need for sleep, irritability, and pressured/loosely associated communication, plus psychotic symptoms including auditory hallucinations, olfactory hallucinations, and ideas of reference/delusional interpretation. Crucially, psychotic symptoms persisted for more than 2 weeks outside of a mood episode, supporting schizoaffective disorder rather than bipolar disorder with psychotic features. Mood episodes have been present for the majority of the total illness duration, and the disturbance has persisted over 6 months with functional decline. No clear major depressive episode was established, and the predominant mood syndrome is manic, consistent with the manic type.
